\begin{document}
\title{From 1965--2025 Barrels Outrun Mass-Based Energy Equivalents, \\But Both Keep Growing}
\author{Karl Svozil \orcidlink{0000-0001-6554-2802}}
\affiliation{Institute for Theoretical Physics, TU Wien,
Wiedner Hauptstra{\ss}e 8-10/136, 1040 Vienna, Austria}
\email{karl.svozil@tuwien.ac.at}
\begin{abstract}
World oil production reaches new highs both in barrels and in a mass-based energy equivalent. Although the energy equivalent per barrel has declined, the total continues to grow.
\end{abstract}
\maketitle

\section{Main finding and scope}
Global oil production sets a new record in 2025 in both volume and reported mass expressed as a standardized energy equivalent. Using the 2026 Energy Institute (EI) edition for every year, volume rises 5.88\% and the daily equivalent 4.70\% above 2018. The equivalent already exceeds 2018 in 2023 and 2024; 2025 extends the record to 100.59~million barrels per day (Mb/d) and 0.53925~exajoules per day (EJ/day). We compare with 2018 because it has the largest gross and net-equivalent daily rates within the common production-and-return window, 1971--2020. Barrel volume first exceeds its 2018 level in 2019. The total daily mass-based energy equivalent has therefore reached new highs despite the decline per barrel.

\textbf{Scope and assumptions.} We assign the same energy content to each reported tonne, so this equivalent tracks mass rather than measured changes in heating value. We then subtract an investment estimate based on joint oil-and-gas returns, allocating inputs to oil in proportion to its assumed output energy. The result tests the historical mass-based series and gives explicit conditions for the years without return data. It does not measure oil-only net energy.

We examine two possible reasons why rising barrel output might coexist with falling energy supply: changes in the stream mix and higher energy requirements for production. The reported natural gas liquids (NGLs) share describes changes in composition; return data and break-even calculations test the investment adjustment under the stated allocation.

\section{Sources, conversions, and time basis}
\subsection{Production and source verification}
We take 1965--2025 world production from the EI 2026 narrow-format dataset, selecting \texttt{Total World} and the variables \texttt{oilprod\_kbd}, \texttt{oilprod\_mt}, \texttt{oilprod\_crudecond\_kbd}, and \texttt{oilprod\_ngl\_kbd} \citep{ei2026}. Matching entries in the EI Excel workbook provide a check on data selection and units. The workbook contains an oil-consumption exajoule series, but no corresponding oil-production exajoule series; Eq.~\eqref{eq:standard} is our conversion of the production mass series. Oil comprises crude oil, tight oil, oil sands, condensates, and gas-plant liquids; biofuels, synthetic liquids from other sources, and refinery processing gain are excluded \citep{eiMethod2026}. Refinery processing gain records a change in product volume, not additional oil extracted.

Appendix~\ref{app:annual} gives every annual value. The reproducibility archive retains the source files and their cryptographic checksums. All years are recalculated from EI 2026, rather than appending 2025 to an older series. A separate comparison with the 2025 release \citep{ei2025,owidEI2025} quantifies the effect of revisions. That earlier extract is preserved in the versioned Our World in Data mirror.

\subsection{Energy equivalent and daily rates}
Let $q_y$ be reported volume in million barrels per day (Mb/d), $M_y$ annual mass in million tonnes (Mt), and $D_y$ the actual number of days in year $y$. Define
\begin{equation}
 G_y^{\rm std}=0.041868M_y\quad\mathrm{EJ},\qquad
 g_y^{\rm std}=G_y^{\rm std}/D_y\quad\mathrm{EJ/day}.
 \label{eq:standard}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{eq:standard} defines a standardized mass-based equivalent rather than measured global heat content. Here EJ means exajoule ($10^{18}$ joules). The factor assigns 41.868 gigajoules (GJ) to each reported tonne. The International Energy Agency (IEA) defines one tonne of oil equivalent (toe) as 41.868~GJ and uses net calorific values in energy balances \citep{ieaBalance,ieaGlossary}. This is a lower-heating-value convention; assigning it to each physical tonne is an assumption, not a claim that one tonne of every oil stream equals one toe. EI's conversion appendix likewise specifies lower heating values \citep{eiGuide2026}.

Throughout, \emph{gross energy} means before subtraction of production-energy inputs. It does not mean higher heating value (HHV). Lower heating value (LHV) excludes heat recovered by condensing combustion water, whereas HHV includes it. The word \emph{net} in net calorific value concerns that heat, while net supply below concerns production inputs.

The equivalent per barrel is
\begin{equation}
 h_y^{\rm std}=\frac{1000G_y^{\rm std}}{q_yD_y}
 \quad\mathrm{GJ/barrel}.
 \label{eq:perbarrel}
\end{equation}
The unit factor is $10^9/10^6=10^3$: one EJ per million barrels equals $10^3$~GJ/barrel. Peak comparisons use daily rates to remove leap-year effects; annual totals remain in the appendix. Relative plots use $100X_y/X_{1971}$. Curves interpolate annual observations with a piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial (PCHIP); all extrema and quoted results use the unsmoothed annual rows.

\subsection{What mass and volume can establish}
The per-barrel equivalent in Eq.~\eqref{eq:perbarrel} is proportional to tonnes per barrel. Its decline therefore records a lower reported mass per barrel, without establishing a change in energy per tonne. Between 1971 and 2025, barrels per tonne rise from approximately 7.43 to 7.81 and the assigned equivalent per barrel falls by 4.82\%.

Let $k_y$ be the actual worldwide mean mass-specific heating value on a consistent LHV basis, and $k_0=41.868$~GJ/t the imposed conversion. The chemical-energy rate implied by the reported mass would be
\begin{equation}
 e_y^{\rm chem}=g_y^{\rm std}\frac{k_y}{k_0}.
 \label{eq:physical}
\end{equation}
From Eq.~\eqref{eq:physical}, 2025 exceeds 2018 in chemical-energy rate if $k_{2025}/k_{2018}>0.9551$. Reversing that ranking therefore requires a fall exceeding 4.49\% in mean heating value per tonne. The standardized decline per barrel measures a change in reported tonnes per barrel, not a change in $k_y$. The source supplies no measured global trajectory for $k_y$. Establishing a record in actual chemical energy would also require comparisons with every other year.

Reported mass can depend on assumptions used to convert volume into tonnes. The downloaded EI methodology does not specify how each national mass series is constructed. National mass--volume ratios do vary: United States barrels per tonne rise from 8.152 in 2005 to 8.640 in 2025 (archived source-reconciliation record). National ratios can change with stream mix, conversion conventions, and revisions; the world ratio also changes with country mix. Even fixed component conversion factors can produce a changing aggregate when component shares change. The reported mass--volume trend alone cannot identify changes in the heating value of individual streams.

A fixed value per tonne also misses differences in mass-specific heating values among streams. EI's illustrative lower heating values are 49.40~GJ/t for ethane and 46.15~GJ/t for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), both above 41.868~GJ/t \citep{eiGuide2026}. If a shift toward these streams raises the mean heating value per tonne, actual energy grows faster than the fixed-factor equivalent. This can partly offset the effect of falling mass per barrel. Quantifying the global correction requires component masses and heating values.

\section{Composition evidence and sensitivity}
For non-overlapping stream flows $V_i$ and heating values per volume $h_i$, let
\begin{equation}
 V=\sum_iV_i,\quad s_i=V_i/V,\quad
 G=V\bar h,\quad \bar h=\sum_i s_ih_i.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\dot G}{G}=\frac{\dot V}{V}+\frac{\dot{\bar h}}{\bar h},\qquad
 \dot{\bar h}=\sum_i\dot s_ih_i+\sum_i s_i\dot h_i.
 \label{eq:composition}
\end{equation}
Here $G$ denotes actual chemical-energy flow in an analytical identity; it is distinct from the standardized statistical equivalent $G_y^{\rm std}$. The first sum is the contribution from changing stream shares; the second is the contribution from changes in each stream's heating value. EI reports the volume shares but not annual global heating values for these streams.

Let $s_L$ be the NGL volume share, with fixed per-barrel heating values $h_C$ for crude plus condensate and $h_L$ for NGLs. Between years $a$ and $b$, the share effect is exactly
\begin{equation}
 \Delta\bar h_{\rm share}=(s_{L,b}-s_{L,a})(h_L-h_C).
 \label{eq:shareeffect}
\end{equation}
For 2018--2025, the observed share increment is 0.02745, so the composition term is $0.02745(h_L-h_C)$. An illustrative ratio $h_L/h_C=0.70$ lowers the mixture's per-barrel value by about 0.85\% relative to 2018. For context, the United States Energy Information Administration (EIA) lists higher-heating-value factors of 3.841 and 4.353~million British thermal units (Btu) per barrel for propane and normal butane \citep{eiaHeat2026}. Dividing by an illustrative crude reference of 5.8~million Btu per barrel gives 0.66 and 0.75. Thus 0.70 represents a plausible propane--butane-rich mixture, rather than an estimated world NGL average. Because these illustrative factors use HHV, this example is kept separate from the LHV-based series. Its effect is not added to the mass-based result, which already incorporates changes in mass per barrel.

\textbf{Small margins and source revisions.}\quad
Table~\ref{tab:vintages} reports edition-specific annual totals and daily rates; the following comparisons distinguish leap-year effects from revisions. In the 2025 edition, the 2024 daily equivalent exceeds 2018 by 0.876\% and 2023 by 0.352\%; annual totals give 1.153\% and 0.627\%. The 2026 edition revises those daily margins to 1.178\% and 0.474\%. Its 2025 daily value exceeds 2018 by 4.704\% and revised 2024 by 3.485\%.

A source revision can reverse a close ranking. If the later estimate is $1+m$ times the earlier one, a downward revision of the later value alone exceeding $m/(1+m)$ reverses it. This threshold is 1.16\% for revised 2024 versus 2018 and 4.49\% for 2025 versus 2018. These cutoffs are sensitivity calculations, not estimates of the probability of a revision.

\subsection{Physical accounting and the conditional oil proxy}
Energy return on investment (EROI), $R$, is returned energy divided by invested energy. For consistently defined flows,
\begin{equation}
 R=G/I,\qquad I=G/R,\qquad N=G-I=G(1-1/R).
 \label{eq:net}
\end{equation}
$G,I,N$ denote gross returned, invested, and net energy under a consistently specified accounting boundary. For additive component outputs and allocated inputs, $1/R=\sum_i w_i/R_i$, where $w_i=G_i/\sum_jG_j$. Aggregate EROI is thus an output-energy-weighted harmonic mean; barrel-weighted averages of the ratios are inappropriate. Joint oil-and-gas extraction requires allocation of shared inputs.

Court and Fizaine reconstruct annual fossil-fuel returns through 2012 using a price-based method \citep{courtFizaine2017}. Hall, Lambert, and Balogh review declining returns and their societal implications, including the possibility that joint oil-and-gas results mask lower oil returns \citep{hallLambertBalogh2014}. Societal minimum-return estimates concern needs beyond extraction; they do not mark a singularity in Eq.~\eqref{eq:net}. We use these studies to compare accounting choices, while retaining a single return series for the historical calculation.

We use Aramendia and colleagues' annual primary-stage oil-and-gas returns for 1971--2020, including direct and indirect requirements \citep{aramendia2024,aramendiaData}. The exact \texttt{global\_erois.csv} selection is world (\texttt{WRLD}), \texttt{Oil and gas products}, \texttt{Primary}, and indirect energy \texttt{Included}. No world oil-only primary-stage row is available; oil-specific rows cover later stages. Applying the joint return to oil gives
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde i_y^{\rm oil}=g_y^{\rm std}/R_y^{OG},\qquad
 \widetilde n_y^{\rm oil}=g_y^{\rm std}-\widetilde i_y^{\rm oil}.
 \label{eq:proxy}
\end{equation}
The superscript $OG$ denotes joint oil and gas. We call $\widetilde n_y^{\rm oil}$ the \emph{net-equivalent proxy}. Its baseline allocation assigns oil the joint system's input energy per unit of output energy. Assigning higher input energy per unit of oil output lowers the adjusted equivalent; assigning less raises it. The source includes indirect supply-chain requirements, uses energy inputs measured at the final stage, and omits capital-formation energy. These are annual-flow, primary-stage returns. Later-stage ratios cannot be inserted into this primary-output calculation; boundary differences across energy-return studies matter \citep{brockway2019,brandt2015}.

The calculation ends at extraction. It does not subtract refining, distribution, or end-use conversion losses.

Table~\ref{tab:investment} displays the subtraction and the direct-only alternative. Joint EROI falls from 41.99 in 1971 to 20.90 in 2007, then stays near 19--22 through 2020. The assumed input deduction rises from 2.38\% in 1971 to 4.79\% in 2020, with annual reversals. Across the full series the retained fraction remains approximately 94.8--97.6\%. The return adjustment lowers the level and modestly reduces growth; it does not turn the long-run rise into a decline. Gross and net-equivalent daily rates both attain their common-window maximum in 2018.

\subsection{How fast must returns fall?}
For differentiable positive gross flow and $R>1$,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\dot N}{N}=\frac{\dot G}{G}+\frac{\dot R}{R(R-1)}.
 \label{eq:netgrowth}
\end{equation}
This follows by differentiating $\ln N=\ln G+\ln(R-1)-\ln R$. If gross energy is increasing and EROI is declining, net energy falls only when
\begin{equation}
 -\frac{\dot R}{R}>(R-1)\frac{\dot G}{G}.
 \label{eq:criterion}
\end{equation}
In plain terms, the fractional loss rate of EROI must exceed $(R-1)$ times the gross growth rate. At $R\simeq21$, it must exceed approximately twenty times that rate. Since $d(N/G)/dR=1/R^2$, the same absolute fall in $R$ removes a larger fraction of gross energy at lower returns. The equation has no singular threshold for $R>1$.

Between 2005 and 2019, joint EROI falls 4.21\% while the daily gross equivalent rises 14.12\%. Over the same interval, the daily net-equivalent proxy rises 13.88\%. The return decline reduces the gain but does not reverse it.

\subsection{Two analytical schematics}
Figure~\ref{fig:schematic}(a) shows the net fraction as a function of return; panel~(b) illustrates a net-energy maximum alongside growing gross output. The example uses a dimensionless progression $s$,
\begin{equation}
 G(s)=G_*e^{gs},\qquad R(s)=R_*e^{-ks},
\end{equation}
with $g,k>0$ and $R>1$. Its stationary point is
\begin{equation}
 s_*=\frac{1}{k}\ln\!\left(\frac{gR_*}{g+k}\right),\qquad
 R(s_*)=1+k/g.
\end{equation}
For $s\ge0$, an interior maximum occurs only if $R_*>1+k/g$. For $g=0.04$, $k=0.40$, and $R_*=20$, the strict maximum occurs at $s_*=1.495$ and $R=11$. Here $k/g=10$ and return falls to about 4.04 by $s=4$. This strong decline illustrates the mechanism; it is not a calibration to the observed return series. Delannoy and colleagues likewise model future net energy using assumed production paths and EROI scenarios \citep{delannoy2021}.

\section{Historical comparisons and missing-year thresholds}
Figure~\ref{fig:relative} compares indexed daily totals and per-barrel equivalents, while Fig.~\ref{fig:absolute} displays the corresponding absolute daily rates. From 1971 to 2025, volume rises 98.07\% and the daily gross equivalent 88.52\%. The standardized equivalent per barrel falls 4.82\%. Over 1971--2020, the net-equivalent proxy grows 63.44\%, compared with 67.58\% for the gross equivalent. Growth in volume has outweighed the per-barrel decline over these intervals. The series also contain contractions, including 1979--1983 and the 2020 pandemic downturn.








The daily net-equivalent proxy reaches 0.49053~EJ/day in 2018 and 0.49013 in 2019, only 0.082\% apart. A downward revision of roughly 0.082\% to the 2018 estimate alone could reverse their order. Moreover, this is a maximum in a proxy based on joint oil-and-gas returns, not a measured oil-only net-energy peak.

\subsection{A quantitative test of the missing years}
For a later year $y$ with a gross equivalent but no published return, the net-equivalent proxy exceeds its 2018 daily value if and only if
\begin{equation}
 R_y^{OG}>R_y^*\equiv
 \left(1-\frac{\widetilde n_{2018}^{\rm oil}}{g_y^{\rm std}}\right)^{-1},
 \label{eq:threshold}
\end{equation}
provided $g_y^{\rm std}>\widetilde n_{2018}^{\rm oil}$. Applying the 2026 production series gives $R_{2024}^*=17.06$ and $R_{2025}^*=11.07$. Equality gives the same daily net proxy; a higher return gives a higher proxy.

To keep the 2025 proxy at or below its 2018 value, the joint return must fall to 11.07 or below, compared with 20.86 in 2020. This is about 47\% below the 2020 value and below every published value in 2005--2020. As a reference scenario, holding the 2020 return constant gives a 2025 proxy of 0.51339~EJ/day, 4.66\% above 2018. For 2018 to remain the proxy's maximum through 2025, input energy per unit of output must therefore increase substantially.

The threshold also depends on the 2018 benchmark. Holding the gross-equivalent ratio fixed, hypothetical 2018 returns of 6 or 8 give 2025 break-even returns of 4.90 or 6.09, respectively. A study using a different accounting boundary must recalculate the output series and both years' inputs before applying this comparison.

\subsection{Sensitivity to the oil allocation}
Let $\alpha_y$ multiply the joint input/output intensity assigned to oil. The baseline has $\alpha_y=1$; values above one represent higher oil intensity. Then
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde n_y(\alpha_y)=g_y^{\rm std}
 \left(1-\frac{\alpha_y}{R_y^{OG}}\right).
 \label{eq:allocation}
\end{equation}
For $0<\alpha_y<R_y^{OG}$ the adjusted equivalent is positive. For a constant $\alpha$ in both comparison years, recompute the 2018 benchmark consistently. When $g_y^{\rm std}>\widetilde n_{2018}(\alpha)$, the proxy exceeds that benchmark if the joint return exceeds
\begin{equation}
 R_y^*(\alpha)=\frac{\alpha}
 {1-\widetilde n_{2018}(\alpha)/g_y^{\rm std}}.
 \label{eq:allocationthreshold}
\end{equation}
For 2025, constant multipliers $\alpha=0.75$, $1$, and $1.25$ give thresholds of 9.50, 11.07, and 12.29. All three thresholds lie below the published 2005--2020 joint-return range. These multipliers are stress tests rather than estimated shares or an uncertainty interval. A time-varying multiplier can change the outcome and requires evidence on oil-specific intensity. Full joint-system reconciliation also requires gas output and consistent allocation of shared inputs.

\section{The 2026 supply shock and the historical cutoff}
The annual production table ends in 2025, before the 2026 Gulf war. It includes production during the Russia--Ukraine conflict, without separating the conflict's effects from other influences.

The IEA's October 2026 report documents disrupted Gulf flows and damage affecting Russian refining and exports \citep{ieaOctober2026}; September had already reported continuing Gulf shut-ins and reduced Russian product exports \citep{ieaSeptember2026}. These reports describe monthly disruptions and near-term forecasts. They supply neither a complete 2026 annual mass series nor matching annual returns, so they are not added to the figures.

War can interrupt production and deliveries while recoverable resources remain. Such a contraction does not by itself demonstrate that depletion or rising extraction-energy requirements have caused a lasting decline. Establishing that claim requires separating those effects from war, policy, and demand. The 2025 record establishes what was produced before the 2026 disruptions; it does not predict future growth or reliable access to supply.

\section{Conclusions}
World oil output reaches new highs in 2025 in both barrels and reported mass expressed as a standardized energy equivalent. Compared with 2018, daily volume rises 5.88\% and the equivalent 4.70\%. Total daily energy equivalent has therefore grown more slowly than barrel volume while reaching a new record. It exceeds every earlier year's daily rate in the 1965--2025 series, ruling out a pre-2025 global maximum in that series.

NGLs account for a growing share of reported oil volume. Because energy per barrel depends on both mass and heating value, the NGL share alone cannot determine the chemical-energy trend. Reversing the 2025--2018 chemical-energy ranking would require a fall exceeding 4.49\% in mean heating value per tonne; the observed volume and mass relationship does not demonstrate that condition.

Declining EROI is likewise insufficient by itself to establish falling net output. With the selected primary-stage return and proportional oil allocation, the 2025 net-equivalent proxy exceeds its 2018 maximum whenever the missing return exceeds 11.07. Keeping the 2025 proxy at or below 2018 requires a return about 47\% below the 2020 value. Constant allocation multipliers from 0.75 to 1.25 give thresholds of 9.50--12.29, all below the published 2005--2020 range.

Testing a chemical-energy peak requires global heating values and documented mass--volume conversions. Testing an oil-only net-energy peak also requires updated oil-specific inputs under a consistent accounting boundary. A claim of an earlier peak must explain how those factors outweigh the observed increase in reported production.
